reformed.atonement:
Reformed Christians teach that Christ's death was a penal substitution: on the cross he bore in our place the punishment that our sins deserve, satisfying God's justice so that God can forgive without ceasing to be just. Salvation therefore rests wholly on what Christ has done, and not on anything we contribute.

Many Reformed churches also teach limited atonement, sometimes called particular redemption. They mean that Christ's death is sufficient for all, but was intended to secure the salvation of those whom the Father has chosen, and that it actually accomplishes what it was meant to do, not merely making salvation possible. This teaching was set out at the Synod of Dort. Some Reformed Christians prefer to speak of a universal offer of the gospel alongside the particular purpose of the cross.
reformed.offices_of_christ:
Reformed teaching describes Christ's work through three offices, an idea often called the threefold office, or in Latin, munus triplex. As prophet, Christ reveals God's will and word. As priest, he offered himself once as a sacrifice for sin and continues to intercede for his people. As king, he rules over the church and the world and will finally defeat every enemy.

This pattern is used in Reformed catechisms and confessions, and is associated with John Calvin's teaching. It is meant to show the fullness of what Christ has done, and to describe the meaning of his name, Christ, which means anointed one: in the Old Testament, prophets, priests and kings were anointed. Reformed Christians find in this a way to praise Christ's full work, and to see his relation to believers as teacher, savior and Lord.
reformed.tongues:
Historically, Reformed churches have taught that the miraculous gift of tongues in the New Testament was a real speaking of known languages, as at Pentecost, and that it served as a sign to confirm the apostles' message in the early days of the church. Many Reformed Christians teach that this gift has ceased.

They also stress the apostle Paul's instructions for order in worship, where what is spoken must be understood and the church built up. Today there are Reformed Christians who are open to the gifts, but the historic and still most common view is that tongues, like other apostolic sign gifts, was given for a particular period. They emphasize that the church's real strength is found in the preaching of the Word and in love, not in such signs.
reformed.continuationism:
The traditional Reformed view is cessationism: the extraordinary gifts of the apostolic age, such as apostolic miracles, new revelation and tongues, ceased when the foundation of the church was laid and Scripture was completed. The Westminster Confession states that the earlier ways of God's revealing his will have now ceased, because Scripture is complete.

This is not a denial that God still acts. Reformed Christians pray for healing, believe God answers prayer, and affirm his providence in all things. Some Reformed teachers today are continuationists, or open but cautious, and hold that gifts like prophecy may still operate, provided they never rival Scripture. The cessationist view remains the historic center of the tradition, but Reformed Christians differ on how firmly it should be held.
reformed.justification:
Reformed churches teach justification by faith alone: God declares sinners righteous, not because of anything they have done, but because Christ's righteousness is credited to them, and their sins are counted against Christ. It is a legal or forensic declaration, a verdict of acquittal and acceptance, which is complete when a person believes.

Faith is not itself the ground of justification, but the instrument by which the sinner receives Christ. Justification cannot be separated from sanctification, the ongoing transformation of the believer's life, which follows as its fruit, though the two are distinct. Good works are the evidence of true faith, not its cause. Reformed Christians consider this teaching central, and one of the main points on which they differ from those who see justification as including inner renewal.
reformed.grace:
Reformed Christians speak of sovereign grace: salvation begins and ends with God's free favor toward sinners who deserve only judgment. Grace is not earned, and it is not merely offered and then left to depend on human response, but it is effective, accomplishing what God intends.

The Holy Spirit brings those whom God has chosen to faith in a way that overcomes their resistance, which is often called effectual or irresistible grace. Because of this the tradition gives all the credit to God. Reformed Christians also speak of common grace, the goodness God shows to all people in providing for them and restraining evil. The phrase doctrines of grace is often used as a name for the Reformed understanding of salvation as God's work from start to finish.
reformed.predestination:
Reformed Christians teach predestination: that before the foundation of the world God freely chose those whom he would save, and that this choice is unconditional, based on his mercy and not on any foreseen faith or merit in the person chosen. Faith itself is understood as a gift which flows from this choice.

This is understood as a source of comfort and humility, and not as a cause for anxiety. It means that salvation is secure, since it rests on God's purpose. Reformed Christians differ on how to speak of those not chosen. Some speak of God passing over them, and others of a corresponding decree. They generally insist that human beings are still responsible for their choices, and that the gospel should be preached to all.
reformed.election:
In Reformed teaching, the elect are those whom God has chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world, as the Letter to the Ephesians says. Election is God's own free choice, not a response to human merit or faith, and it is the origin of the calling, faith and perseverance of believers.

Reformed Christians are careful not to guess who the elect are. The gospel is preached to everyone, and anyone who believes may be sure that God has chosen him. Election is treated mainly as a doctrine of comfort and thanksgiving: that a person's salvation depends on God and cannot fail. It is also a call to humility and to holiness, since the elect are chosen in order to be holy.
reformed.perseverance:
Reformed churches teach the perseverance of the saints: that those whom God has truly called and saved will continue in faith to the end and will not finally be lost. This is because God keeps them by his power, and the Holy Spirit who has begun the work will finish it.

It is not that believers never struggle or fall into serious sin. They may stumble, and Scripture warns them to take care, but the tradition holds that God will restore them. Those who finally fall away are taken to be people who never truly belonged to Christ, though they appeared to. The doctrine is sometimes summarized as preservation by God, and is meant to give confidence that salvation depends on his faithfulness.
reformed.assurance:
Reformed churches teach that believers can be assured of their salvation. Such assurance rests first on the promises of God in the gospel, then on the inward witness of the Holy Spirit, and also on the fruit of a changed life. It is a gift to be sought, and believers are urged to make their calling and election sure.

The Westminster Confession adds that this assurance is not part of the essence of faith, so a true believer may wait long for it and may lose it for a time through sin or temptation. They may still be truly saved. Reformed pastors therefore encourage the doubting to look to Christ and to the promises and not to their own feelings. It differs from views that say no one can know their standing before death.
reformed.means_of_grace:
Reformed Christians speak of the means of grace: the ordinary ways God uses to give and strengthen faith. The Westminster Shorter Catechism names the Word, the sacraments and prayer as the outward means by which Christ communicates the benefits of redemption.

The preaching of the Word is central. The two sacraments, Baptism and the Lord's Supper, are signs and seals of the promises of the gospel. These means work not by any power in themselves but through the Holy Spirit, and by faith. They are the ordinary channels, though God is free to work in other ways. Reformed Christians therefore emphasize regular attendance at the worship of the church, where the means are used together.
reformed.original_sin:
Reformed churches teach that Adam was the representative head of the human race, an idea called federal headship: in his disobedience all his descendants are counted guilty, and all inherit a corrupt nature. They draw on the Letter to the Romans, which sets Adam and Christ side by side as two heads of humanity.

Because of this, everyone is born guilty and with a nature inclined to evil, and cannot save themselves. Salvation is likewise understood in terms of Christ's headship: those united to him receive his righteousness as Adam's descendants receive his sin. Reformed Christians thus hold that both the problem and the solution are matters of representation. Some traditions describe original sin mainly as inherited corruption, and Reformed teaching typically includes both guilt and corruption.
reformed.free_will:
Reformed Christians teach the bondage of the will: because of sin, the human will is enslaved, so that people in their natural state freely choose according to their sinful desires and will not turn to God unless he changes them. They are still responsible for what they choose, since they choose willingly, and no one is forced to sin.

Reformed Christians use the term free agency for this: people act voluntarily, but their will is not neutral. Only when God renews the heart by his Spirit are they freed to love and follow him. This is why the tradition speaks of regeneration, the new birth, as coming before faith and enabling it. It differs from teaching in which grace restores a neutral ability to choose, and Reformed teachers often refer to Martin Luther's writing on the bondage of the will as an expression of the same conviction.
reformed.total_depravity:
Reformed churches teach total depravity, sometimes called total inability. It does not mean that every person is as evil as possible. It means that sin has affected every part of a person, including the mind, will and affections, so that no one can save himself or even truly desire God without God's grace.

Reformed Christians also affirm that unbelievers can do good in a civil and social sense, because of common grace, which restrains sin and gives gifts to all people. What they cannot do, by their own strength, is to please God in the sense of loving him above all and trusting Christ. The doctrine is intended to show that salvation must be entirely God's work, and it is often the starting point for the rest of the Reformed account of grace.
reformed.sola_scriptura:
Reformed churches hold that Scripture alone is the final authority in matters of faith and life. The Westminster Confession states that the whole counsel of God is either expressly set down in Scripture, or may by good and necessary consequence be deduced from it, and that nothing is to be added to it.

Reformed churches value confessions and catechisms, such as the Heidelberg Catechism and the Westminster Standards, which summarize what Scripture teaches, and they honor the teaching of the early church. Yet these are subordinate standards which are tested by Scripture, and can be corrected by it. The Holy Spirit is understood to persuade believers of the truth and authority of Scripture through the Word itself. This differs from teaching in which tradition or a teaching office stands beside Scripture as an equal authority.
reformed.hermeneutics:
Reformed interpreters hold that Scripture is its own best interpreter: the rule for understanding a difficult passage is to compare it with other parts of the Bible, letting the clearer passages shed light on the darker ones. This is called the analogy of faith, and rests on the belief that Scripture, though written by many people, has one divine author and does not contradict itself.

The Westminster Confession says that the infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is Scripture itself. Reformed readers also read the whole Bible as pointing to Christ, and pay attention to context, language and the way God's covenant unfolds. Creeds and the teachings of the church are used as aids, not as authorities above Scripture. The aim is to let the whole Bible speak with a consistent voice.
reformed.visible_and_invisible_church:
Reformed churches distinguish between the invisible church and the visible church. The invisible church is the whole number of the elect, gathered from every age and place, known fully only to God. The visible church consists of all those throughout the world who profess the true religion, together with their children, organized in local congregations.

Both are real, and both are the church of Christ. The visible church is mixed, and contains some who are not truly believers, as Jesus' parable of the wheat and the weeds describes. It is marked by the preaching of the Word, the right administration of the sacraments and, in many Reformed statements, by discipline. Believers are expected to join and support a local visible church, even though they know it is imperfect.
reformed.elders:
In Reformed churches, elders are the leaders who govern and care for the congregation. Elders are chosen from among the members and ordained, and together they oversee the doctrine and life of the church, visit and counsel members, and exercise discipline. In many Reformed churches they meet as a consistory or session, together with the pastor.

The tradition, following John Calvin, recognizes offices of pastor, teacher, elder and deacon. Pastors and teachers are responsible for the Word, and elders share in rule and shepherding, while deacons care for the poor and for mercy ministries. The conviction is that Christ rules his church through Scripture and through leaders who serve together and are accountable to one another, so that no single person holds all authority.
reformed.infant_baptism:
Reformed churches baptize the infant children of believers. They teach that the sign of the covenant of grace, which in the Old Testament was circumcision, is now baptism, and that God's promises extend to believers and to their children, as the apostle Peter says in Acts. Baptism is therefore a sign and seal of God's promise, and of belonging to his people.

Reformed churches do not teach that baptism automatically regenerates a child. The promise must be received by faith, and parents promise to raise the child in the faith. This is sometimes called covenant baptism. It differs from Baptists, who baptize only professing believers, and from teaching in which baptism itself imparts new life. Reformed churches also baptize adults who come to faith and have not been baptized.
reformed.real_presence:
Reformed Christians, following John Calvin, teach that Christ is truly present in the Lord's Supper, but spiritually and not physically. The bread and wine remain bread and wine, and yet by the work of the Holy Spirit believers who receive them in faith are truly fed with Christ himself, and are united to him.

Calvin described it as the Spirit lifting believers up to heaven, where Christ is, to feed on him there. The Supper is therefore not a mere memorial, as some Christians teach, and not a change in the elements, as others teach. It is a sacrament in which God really gives what he promises. Views within the wider Reformed family have varied, and some individuals hold a more memorial view, but the confessional Reformed teaching is this spiritual presence received by faith.
reformed.icons:
Reformed churches teach that God is to be worshiped only in the way that he has commanded in Scripture, and that the Second Commandment forbids making images to worship or to represent God in worship. For this reason, the Reformers removed statues and paintings from churches, and Reformed worship is centered on the Word, the sacraments and prayer.

They hold that God has given his own images for worship: the preaching of the Word and the sacraments. Reformed Christians do not oppose art in itself, and many value it in daily life, but they do not use images or icons in worship or as objects of veneration. How strictly the principle is applied differs, and some Reformed churches today have more decoration than in earlier times, but the historic conviction is against images in worship.
reformed.preaching:
Reformed churches give preaching a central place in worship. They teach that when the Word of God is faithfully preached, God himself speaks to his people, and the sermon is a means by which the Holy Spirit creates and strengthens faith. The Second Helvetic Confession expresses this by saying that the preaching of the Word of God is the Word of God.

For this reason the pulpit is usually the focus of the sanctuary, and Reformed pastors are trained to explain and apply the text of Scripture, often preaching through whole books of the Bible in order. The sermon is normally long and doctrinal, and is meant to teach as well as to move. Reformed Christians regard the faithful preaching of the Word as one of the marks of a true church.
reformed.perpetual_virginity:
Reformed Christians confess the virgin birth of Jesus, and honor Mary as the mother of the Lord. On the question of whether she remained a virgin all her life, the tradition has not been uniform. Some early Reformed teachers, such as Zwingli, held that she did, but this is not a confessional teaching.

Many Reformed Christians today read the passages that speak of the brothers of the Lord as referring to Jesus' younger siblings, the children of Mary and Joseph, since this is the most natural reading of the text. Others regard the question as open, since Scripture does not settle it clearly. Reformed churches do not pray to Mary, and they place the emphasis on what her story shows about Christ, and they do not make the perpetual virginity a matter of doctrine.
